10_targets: Four of the five columns the CSV declares as targets. Only next-workout RPE was ever trained; the other three are written by the rule code in inference_worker.py at inference time, not predicted by a model. Note the injury-risk panel never exceeds 0.86 - that is the heuristic's clip ceiling, not a learned distribution.
11_focus_classes: The focus label is not a free choice the model must discover - each class occupies its own RPE band, so an RPE regression already encodes most of it. That is why a focus classifier would look accurate while adding little.
12_correlations: Readiness dominates. readiness_composite_score alone carries the strongest linear relationship with the target, which is what the next stage's feature importance will confirm - and what makes the leakage question in figure 14 worth asking.
13_integrity: The dataset is clean and evenly shaped - which is exactly what a generated dataset looks like. Only 9% of the target's variance sits between athletes, so the model is not really learning “who recovers slowly”; it is learning day-to-day response. That is the right thing for a daily prescription, and the wrong thing to reuse as a season-level readiness forecast.
14_leakage: This is the chart to argue about. The target is next week's average RPE, and the features include this week's RPE and today's readiness. An athlete who trains hard this week reports high readiness stress and high RPE, and tends to train hard next week too - so the model can score well by learning persistence rather than physiology. It is not a leak of the future, but it is why the headline R² is not a measure of predictive skill.
20_metrics: Grey is what the bundle reports - the model scored on the rows it memorised. Orange is a held-out final 20% of the season. Teal is the floor any model must clear: predicting the club average, and predicting each athlete's own last seven days. The gap between grey and orange is the honest cost of asking the model about something it has not already seen.
21_actual_vs_predicted: The diagonal is a perfect forecast. A useful model hugs it. Points spread horizontally along a row are the same true value predicted differently; points stacked vertically are athletes whose week the model could not anticipate.
22_residuals: Near-zero mean bias and a narrow spread looks healthy - and it is, on the range the model has seen. The risk is extrapolation: coaches will use this on athletes outside these 50 days, and gradient-boosted trees cannot predict outside the values they were shown.
23_learning_curve: Where the curve flattens is where more of the same data stopped helping. If it is already flat at the left edge, the ceiling is the feature set - not the sample size - and collecting another season of the same columns will not fix it.
32_shap_global: SHAP is measured in the model's own units, so these are RPE points: a one-athlete change in readiness moves the forecast by roughly the value shown. Compare that with the held-out MAE of ~0.36 - if a single feature can move the answer by more than the model's own error, that feature is doing almost all of the work.
30_importance_by_family: Readiness and load together own most of the model. Demographics and event group - the things a coach cannot change today - contribute little, which is the right shape for a daily prescription tool.
31_importance_detail: Left is how often the trees used a column; right is how much accuracy the model loses without it. A feature can be used constantly and matter little (it is a cheap proxy for something else). Where the two rankings disagree, the right-hand one is the trustworthy one.
33_pdp: Every input except the one on the x-axis is frozen at its median. This is how the model responds to that feature in isolation - the shape a coach needs when they ask ‘what happens if he sleeps badly tonight?’. Flat segments mean the model does not use that range; steps mean it splits on a threshold.
34_contributions: Read bottom to top: start from the model's baseline (the average prediction it would make knowing nothing), then add each feature's push. Orange pushes the prescription harder, blue eases it. This is the exact arithmetic behind one athlete's number - it is not a separate, approximate explanation.
42_input_audit: Red inputs are identical for every athlete in this sample, so they cannot change the answer. Two are structural: base_fitness_score is the contract's fallback of 75 because every club percentile comes back as exactly 50, and training_age is 0.03 years - eleven days, the age of the database row rather than years in the sport. Periodisation dummies are constant because the phase is club-wide. The injury flags are only zero because none of these six athletes is currently injured.
40_decision_path: Read left to right: data becomes features, features become 31 columns, and those become one number - the predicted RPE. Everything after that point is deterministic code. It is not wrong to combine a model with rules (a safety layer should be rules), but the numbers labelled injury risk and progression come from the green column, not from XGBoost.
41_athlete_cards: Each card is built by running the production heuristics on live pipeline features - these are the real strings and numbers the app would store. Notice how much of each card is text generated by thresholds, and how little of it varies the model's output.
43_stored_outputs: Read straight from the recommendations collection. A recommendation tagged rules-cold-start-v1 was produced because ML inference failed or was unavailable - the backend falls back silently and still shows a confidence number. If you want coaches to trust the feature, the origin should be visible on screen, and a failed inference should be an error state rather than a plausible-looking substitute.
50_acwr_definition: workload.py divides a seven-day total by a twenty-eight-day total, so steady training reads about 0.25 - the right-hand panel shows the arithmetic. The 0.8 / 1.3 / 1.5 thresholds in the injury-risk and progression rules assume a ratio scaled the other way, where 1.0 means steady. On the shipped scale the “spike” branches cannot fire and the “undertrained” branch is almost always true. In the dev database the effect is masked because almost no athlete-day clears the eight-session guard.
51_trajectories: Teal is load ratio, orange dots are how hard each session actually felt. Most athletes never leave the dashed band, and the caption in each panel is how many days had fewer than eight sessions in the trailing month - the threshold at which the engine stops trusting its own load ratio.
52_readiness_vs_rpe: Left: in train_data.csv, fresher athletes report clearly lower effort (r = -0.65), and readiness is the model's heaviest input. Right: the same composite built from the dev database's 332 real check-ins shows no relationship at all (r = -0.02). Either the seeded history is random, or the effect is smaller than the synthetic data claims. Both mean this database cannot currently validate the model - and neither can a coach's trust be earned from a correlation that only exists in generated data.
53_competition_labels: A “will they be ready on the day” model needs labelled competition outcomes. Three competitions is a sample you can describe, not one you can learn from. This is the constraint that decides the phasing of the prediction feature.
